- My aim for the previous turn was achieved, as we successfully separated the models based on product and catalyst dependencies. Now, the goal is to definitively distinguish between the specific higher-order catalyst mechanisms (M2 vs M5) while continuing to isolate them from standard (M1) or deactivation (M13, M19) models.

<hypothesis>
To strongly differentiate between M2 (inactive catalyst dimerization) and M5 (catalysis requiring a second free catalyst molecule), we should move to a stoichiometric or "single-turnover" regime where the initial catalyst concentration exceeds the substrate concentration. 
By setting a very low substrate concentration (S=0.1) and the maximum catalyst concentration (cat=0.2) with no initial product (P=0.0), the system will have an abundance of free catalyst throughout the reaction. 
In this regime, M5 will proceed extremely rapidly because the abundant free catalyst will strongly drive the `catS + cat <=> catP + cat` step. Conversely, in M2, the high concentration of free catalyst will drive the formation of the inactive dimer (`2cat <=> cat2`), significantly reducing the active catalyst pool and slowing the reaction relative to M5. Furthermore, this condition will clearly separate bimolecular catalyst deactivation (M13) from standard kinetics (M1), as the high free catalyst concentration will maximize the deactivation rate in M13. Removing the initial product ensures we isolate these catalyst-centric effects without confounding product inhibition.
</hypothesis>
